questions.stem: Which Fundamental Duty under Article 51A specifically requires every citizen to 'develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform'?

options.option_text: Clause (h) — scientific temper duty
Clause (e) — harmony and brotherhood duty
Clause (g) — environment protection duty
Clause (j) — excellence striving duty

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 51A(h) — 'to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.' This clause reflects JAWAHARLAL NEHRU's vision from 'Discovery of India' (1946) — Nehru himself coined the phrase 'scientific temper.' Clause (e) = promote harmony, renounce derogatory practices against women. Clause (g) = protect natural environment. Clause (j) = strive towards excellence. UPSC ANGLE: Maharashtra Anti-Superstition & Black Magic Act 2013 draws legislative force from Art 51A(h). Courts have used this clause to strike down practices labelled 'unscientific' — e.g., banning dolphin shows (Bombay HC 2016 referenced scientific temper). PYQ FREQUENCY: appears 1-2× per UPSC Prelims cycle, regularly in SSC CGL GK and TNPSC. EXAM TRAP: students confuse (h) with (g) environment; remember — (g) = Green/environment, (h) = Head/Scientific thinking. MEMORY AID: 'H for Head = think with your Head = scientific temper'.

questions.stem: The 11th Fundamental Duty — added by the 86th Amendment, 2002 — places responsibility on parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to children aged:

options.option_text: 6 to 14 years (linked to Art 21A Right to Education)
5 to 16 years (aligned with UNICEF child-labour norms)
6 to 18 years (full secondary school completion)
4 to 14 years (early childhood inclusion)

questions.explanation: 86th AMENDMENT (2002) inserted: (1) Art 21A — Right to Education as a Fundamental Right for children aged 6-14. (2) Art 51A(k) — Fundamental Duty of parents/guardians to provide education opportunities for children aged 6-14. (3) Amended Art 45 (DPSP) to extend care & education for children below 6. The 6-14 age bracket matches the Right to Education Act 2009. UPSC ANGLE: 86th Amendment was a watershed — it converted what was a DPSP (Art 45, non-justiciable) into a justiciable Fundamental Right (Art 21A). The corresponding FD (Art 51A(k)) is non-justiciable but creates a moral duty. PYQ FREQUENCY: age bracket 6-14 appears in every competitive exam cycle — UPSC, SSC, banking. EXAM TRAP: 5-16 and 6-18 are common distractors; the exact bracket is 6 to 14, not one year more or less. MEMORY AID: '6 se 14 tak — RTE ka saath' (6 to 14 — with RTE).

questions.stem: Which of the following existing laws is commonly cited as giving legislative backing to the Fundamental Duty of 'safeguarding public property and abjuring violence' (Article 51A(i))?

options.option_text: Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984
Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (not this)
Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967

questions.explanation: ARTICLE 51A(i) — 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence.' The PREVENTION OF DAMAGE TO PUBLIC PROPERTY ACT, 1984 directly enforces this duty — it penalises wilful damage to public property including during hartals and protests. The Supreme Court in 2009 (Re: Destruction of Public & Private Properties v. State of AP) reinforced this connection and gave guidelines on making protest organisers liable for damage. OTHER DUTY-LEGISLATION MAP: Art 51A(a) — respect Constitution/flag/anthem → Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971. Art 51A(c) — defend the country → Military conscription laws. Art 51A(e) — renounce practices derogatory to women → Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. UPSC ANGLE: Javed Akhtar PIL (2007) in SC linked public property protection to fundamental duties doctrine. PYQ FREQUENCY: high in SSC CHSL, UPSC Prelims option sets. MEMORY AID: (i) = Infrastructure protection = Property Damage Act.

questions.stem: Fundamental Duties under the Indian Constitution apply to:

options.option_text: Only citizens of India (not foreigners residing in India)
All persons in Indian territory including foreign nationals
Only those citizens who have taken an oath of allegiance
Citizens and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) card holders

questions.explanation: FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Art 51A) apply ONLY TO CITIZENS — unlike Fundamental Rights, where some rights (Art 14 equality, Art 21 life/liberty) extend to all persons including foreigners. This is a critical distinction tested frequently. CONTRAST: Fundamental Rights — Art 15/16/19/30 only for citizens; Art 14/20/21/22 for all persons. Fundamental Duties — exclusively for citizens. UPSC ANGLE: The distinction matters in PIL litigation — a foreign national cannot be compelled under FD basis; however, courts may apply other statutory frameworks. No provision imposes FDs on Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) — OCI is not a full citizenship category (no voting rights either). PYQ FREQUENCY: citizen vs person distinction appears 2-3× per year across UPSC, MPSC, SSC. EXAM TRAP: Option B is the classic wrong answer — students assume since Art 21 applies to 'persons', FDs also do; they don't. MEMORY AID: 'Duties are for Desis (citizens); Rights are broader.'

questions.stem: In AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS (2002), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Duties:

options.option_text: Must be taken into account while testing the constitutional validity of a law (given equal weight as DPSPs)
Are directly enforceable against citizens through writ petitions (not this) instead
Override Fundamental Rights when there is a conflict between the two (not this) instead
Are purely political declarations and have no legal significance whatsoever (not this)

questions.explanation: AIIMS STUDENTS' UNION v. AIIMS (2002) — landmark SC judgment on Fundamental Duties. The court held: FDs are NOT mere moral precepts; courts MUST keep them in mind while interpreting laws and testing their constitutional validity. They are placed on par with DPSPs — used as an interpretive tool, not a ground for direct enforcement. KEY HOLDING: 'It is the duty of the court to evolve, affirm and adopt principles that will further the fundamental duties.' FDs ≠ directly enforceable (you cannot file a writ saying someone violated a FD against you). FDs do NOT override FRs — FRs are supreme if there's genuine conflict. UPSC ANGLE: This case is the ONLY major SC authority directly interpreting the legal weight of FDs as a class. Compare with DPSPs — Art 37 explicitly says DPSPs 'shall not be enforceable by any court' yet states 'it shall be the duty of the state to apply these principles.' FDs have no such explicit clause — their non-justiciability is inferred. PYQ FREQUENCY: case appears in UPSC CSE Mains GS-2, State PSC Mains.

questions.stem: Which country's constitution served as the primary inspiration for including a list of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution via the 42nd Amendment, 1976?

options.option_text: USSR (Soviet Union — 1977 Constitution listed citizen duties in Articles 60–69)
USA (Bill of Rights implies civic obligations alongside individual rights)
Japan (post-war 1947 Constitution has Article 12 on citizen responsibilities)
France (Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen 1789 mentioned duties)

questions.explanation: USSR CONSTITUTION (specifically the 1936 Stalin Constitution and later 1977 Brezhnev Constitution, Articles 60-69) served as the explicit model for India's FDs. The SWARAN SINGH COMMITTEE (1976) recommended FDs after studying socialist constitutions. The Emergency era government under Indira Gandhi was ideologically aligned with the Soviet model. The 42nd Amendment also added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble — reinforcing the USSR influence. Japan's Art 12 does mention 'citizen's duty to maintain freedoms' but is not the cited source. France's 1789 Declaration mentions duties alongside rights but is more rights-focused. UPSC ANGLE: USSR dissolved in 1991, but Russian Federation Constitution (1993) retained some duty clauses. China (Art 54), Vietnam, Cuba — socialist constitutions similarly embed duties. India is unusual among major democracies in having an explicit duties list. PYQ FREQUENCY: sourcing FDs to USSR appears in UPSC Prelims, SSC CGL, BPSC. EXAM TRAP: Japan is the most plausible distractor since Japan also has constitutional duties language and a democratic constitution.

questions.stem: Justice Verma Committee (1999) on Fundamental Duties recommended that Fundamental Duties should be operationalised through education. Which of its findings is most accurately stated?

options.option_text: All 11 Fundamental Duties have at least one existing law that gives them legislative backing
Only 6 of the 11 duties have legislative backing; the rest are purely aspirational
Fundamental Duties should be elevated to justiciable rights via a constitutional amendment
A National Tribunal for Enforcement of Duties should be established under Article 323B

questions.explanation: JUSTICE J.S. VERMA COMMITTEE (1999) — key findings: (1) All 11 Fundamental Duties ARE backed by at least one existing piece of legislation. (2) Recommended a 'compendium' mapping each duty to its existing law. (3) Recommended teaching FDs in schools via the curriculum. (4) Recommended establishing a 'National Foundation for Fundamental Rights and Duties' (not a tribunal). The committee did NOT recommend making FDs justiciable or creating new enforcement tribunals. Examples of the legislation mapping: Art 51A(a) flag/anthem → National Honour Act 1971; Art 51A(b) freedom struggle ideals → no specific Act but spirit embedded in Preamble; Art 51A(g) environment → Environment Protection Act 1986, Wildlife Protection Act 1972; Art 51A(i) public property → Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act 1984. UPSC ANGLE: This committee finding is used in judicial reasoning — courts invoke existing laws to give FDs indirect enforceability without requiring a constitutional amendment. PYQ FREQUENCY: Verma Committee findings appear in UPSC Mains GS-2 and MPSC Prelims.
